📌 Seed Phrase Storage: Why a Screenshot Is a Wallet Left Open

Main Points
⏺ Your seed phrase is the master key — whoever has it controls the wallet
⏺ Photos, screenshots and notes apps quietly copy it into the cloud
⏺ This post explains where seed phrases leak and how to store one safely


1⃣ Core Idea — A seed phrase can restore your wallet on any device. Anyone who sees those 12 or 24 words can do the same, without your password or your phone.
2⃣ Why It Happens — A screenshot feels private, but photo galleries, notes and email drafts often sync automatically to cloud accounts.
3⃣ Example — Someone saves a screenshot "just in time". Months later their cloud account is compromised, and the wallet is emptied the same day.
4⃣ Risk Surface — Cloud backups, password-reset phishing, infostealer malware that scans images and text files, and shared or lost devices.
5⃣ Practical Rule — Write the phrase on paper or metal, keep it offline in a safe place, and never type or photograph it. A real wallet will never ask for it to "verify" anything.
Final Thoughts

Your wallet is only as safe as the place where your seed phrase lives. If it ever touched a phone camera or a cloud folder, treat it as exposed and move funds to a new wallet.

Democrats are returning to Capitol Hill with increased political leverage and a growing list of investigations and legislative priorities.

The battle over government funding is another urgent issue. Congress must approve a funding package by mid-December to prevent another federal government shutdown.

Lawmakers also face negotiations over the annual defense authorization bill, which sets Pentagon policy and includes military spending priorities. Disagreements over funding for the Iran war and military assistance to Israel could complicate negotiations.
Republicans also face a shrinking window to advance Trump's judicial nominees before Democrats assume control of the Senate in January.

The political consequences could be significant. A Democratic-controlled Congress will have greater authority to conduct investigations, hold hearings, demand documents and challenge administration policies.

For Trump, the challenge is no longer simply defending his legislative agenda. He must also prepare for a more aggressive congressional opposition during the second half of his term.

Today's Speech Summary... 

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh just warned that the AI boom could end in a stock market crash and rising unemployment.

In his remark today, Warsh discussed what could happen if the AI boom doesn't go as investors expect.

Companies have already invested heavily in AI, but if the returns disappoint, stock prices could fall and the US economy could slow down.

And even if AI succeeds, things might not be much better for workers.

Warsh warned that automation could replace jobs on a large scale, pushing unemployment higher even if the economy continues growing.

He also raised concerns about AI being used to attack critical infrastructure, like we saw with the Houthis' attack on the Middle East.

But that's a good thing in the long run.

Slow economic growth and high unemployment will force the Fed to bring rates down and start QE just like we saw in 2020-21, which will send markets to astronomical highs.

Early Christmas decorating may boost happiness by bringing back positive memories and encouraging social connection.

Psychotherapist Amy Morin, author of 13 Things Mentally Strong People Don't Do, told Good Morning America that familiar decorations can rekindle the warmth of childhood holidays. Putting them up early may extend those joyful feelings over more weeks.

There are social benefits as well. In a 1989 Journal of Environmental Psychology study, people viewing photos of decorated homes saw even less outgoing homeowners as friendlier and more sociable. Morin adds that festive displays can start conversations with neighbors, while seasonal generosity supports happiness.

[Werner, C. M., Peterson-Lewis, S., & Brown, B. B. (1989). Inferences about homeowners' sociability: Impact of Christmas decorations and other cues. Journal of Environmental Psychology, 9(4), 279–296. DOI: 10.1016/S0272-4944(89)80010-6]
